searched: Read _design-system/LOCKFILE.md sections 0 and 1 (color tokens, hard rules, RETIRED list) end to end, _design-system/CANON.md (19 lines, short), _design-system/DRIFT_LEDGER.md (structure-drift, not color), and grepped RATIONALE.md and research/TASTE_RANGE.md for CVD/contrast/token-count language. Read tailwind.config.js lines 1-260 (the full colors block) and app/globals.css color-variable sections. Counted every top-level s- token (47) with `grep -oE '"s-[a-zA-Z0-9-]+"' tailwind.config.js`, then checked live usage of each across app/components/components-legacy/lib with per-token grep passes (both a strict prefixed-class regex and a plain substring pass to catch border-l-s-cal-hair-style compounds). Read the drift-check enforcement source directly (.claude/skills/solen-drift-check/scripts/check.py, the RETIRED_TOKENS/ALLOWED_HEX/HEX_RE/A1/A5/A15 logic and DEFAULT_SCAN_GLOBS) rather than trusting the skill's own description. Grepped for contrast/WCAG/colorblind/forced-colors coverage across _design-system and _rules. Searched non-Tailwind color surfaces: lib/email-templates/*.ts, lib/email.ts, and app/api/salon/invoices/[payoutId]/route.ts (found by `find . -iname '*invoice*' -o -iname '*email*'`), reading the actual hex literals inside their template strings. Grepped app/components for `from-[#...]`/`to-[#...]` arbitrary gradient hex to find duplicated literal palettes. Checked _design-system/REMOVED.md and TASTE_LOG.md for token/amber/invoice/email/contrast/gradient hits before writing any finding, and confirmed LOCKFILE's RETIRED section wording against the live tailwind.config.js token names. Did not find a colorblind-accessibility gap (RATIONALE.md section 3 already carries T1 CVD-prevalence math and 'color never sole carrier' is enforced in components like ProgressStepper) or a text-on-photo-scrim gap (DS-10 scrim recipe in LOCKFILE is thorough) so neither is reported as missing.

findings.title: Retired-token enforcement list has drifted from the tokens it is supposed to block
findings.principle: Whenever a token is added to LOCKFILE.md's RETIRED list, the same commit must add the EXACT token name (as it appears in tailwind.config.js) to check.py's RETIRED_TOKENS set, and a CI/pre-commit check must diff the two lists and fail if they disagree. A retired-token name that does not match a real tailwind.config.js key is worse than no entry: it gives false confidence that enforcement exists.
findings.why: The drift-checker's RETIRED_TOKENS set is the only mechanical thing standing between 'we said this token is dead' and a new PR quietly reusing it. If the set names tokens that do not exist, it enforces nothing while looking like it enforces something, and nobody notices because the report never fires.
findings.local_evidence: LOCKFILE.md's RETIRED section (around line 118) lists the dead atmosphere family as `s-atm-*` and separately says `s-amber` was 'PERMANENTLY KILLED V3-D320'. The actual tailwind.config.js tokens (verified lines 112-116) are `s-atm-cream`, `s-atm-terra`, `s-atm-sage`, `s-atm-bone`, `s-atm-butter`. But check.py's RETIRED_TOKENS set (lines 108-127) instead lists `s-atm-warm`, `s-atm-cool`, `s-atm-base` -- names that do not exist anywhere in tailwind.config.js -- and never lists `s-amber` at all. Result: `grep -rl "\bs-amber\b" app components components-legacy lib` returns 19 files (e.g. app/[locale]/dashboard/discovery-admin/page.tsx:186, app/[locale]/dashboard/admin-sandbox/page.tsx:186-492, components-legacy/dashboard/coiffeur/FormulaBook.tsx:168, components-legacy/loyalty/StampCard.tsx, components-legacy/dashboard/ActivityFeed.tsx, components/ui/BackgroundBlobs.tsx, components/ui/BlobBackground.tsx) actively using a token the LOCKFILE calls dead, and the drift-checker cannot see any of it because its list points at fictional names.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 's-amber\|s-atm-cream\|s-atm-terra\|s-atm-sage\|s-atm-bone\|s-atm-butter\|s-love' .claude/skills/solen-drift-check/scripts/check.py -> zero hits. grep -rn 'retired.*sync\|token.*audit\|verify retired' _design-system _rules CLAUDE.md -> no hits; nothing checks the two lists against each other.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: LOCKFILE.md's RETIRED section (documentation) correctly names s-amber and the real s-atm-* tokens as dead. The gap is entirely in the enforcement layer (check.py), which never got updated to match, and there is no process that keeps the two in sync.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md (add a one-line rule under the RETIRED section) + .claude/skills/solen-drift-check/scripts/check.py (fix RETIRED_TOKENS immediately: replace s-atm-warm/cool/base with the real 5 names, add s-amber and s-love)
findings.enforcement: gate: retired-token-sync-check -- a small script that parses tailwind.config.js token keys and LOCKFILE.md's RETIRED bullet list, and fails if a LOCKFILE-retired token name has no exact match in check.py's RETIRED_TOKENS

findings.title: Server-rendered, printed financial documents (payout invoices) are entirely outside the token system
findings.principle: Any surface that generates its own HTML/CSS string outside the React/Tailwind component tree (email templates, printable invoices, PDF exports, webhooks that render HTML) must import its colors and font stack from one shared, versioned constants file that mirrors the LOCKFILE hex table (e.g. lib/brand-constants.ts), never inline a fresh hex or a generic font-family. A financial document a partner can print or save as PDF is not exempt from brand and legibility law just because it cannot use Tailwind classes.
findings.why: The token system's entire value is that one color decision (a rebrand, a contrast fix, a retirement) propagates everywhere automatically. A hand-rolled HTML string with its own hex values is a second, silent source of truth that the token system's owner does not know exists and cannot update by editing tailwind.config.js.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/salon/invoices/[payoutId]/route.ts (the salon commission payout statement, with an explicit `<button onclick="window.print()">Drucken / PDF speichern</button>` at line 59, i.e. a document partners are meant to print or save) uses `color: #333` (line 43) instead of s-ink `#0A0A0A`, `background: #f9f9f9` (line 48) instead of s-bg-sunken `#F4F4F5`, `color: #666` (line 122) instead of s-ink-2 `#6B6B6B`, `font-family: sans-serif` (line 43) instead of Inter/Inter Tight (the LOCKFILE's 'never Geist... Inter Tight + Inter only' rule), and a brand color `#C05038` (lines 44, 45, 51, 59, 110, 114) that matches NO token in the LOCKFILE §1 table at all -- it is a rust/terracotta hue from no era of the palette history documented in tailwind.config.js's own comments.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'invoice\|receipt\|pdf\|print' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md -> no hits for any print/PDF/invoice color governance. grep -n '@media print' app/globals.css -> zero results, confirming no print stylesheet exists anywhere to have caught this.
findings.existing_coverage: none. The DEFAULT_SCAN_GLOBS in check.py do include `app/**/*.ts`, which technically covers this file's extension, but nobody has run/reviewed the scan against it (the hex #C05038/#333/#f9f9f9/#666 are not in ALLOWED_HEX, so a scan would flag them as A1 hard findings, yet they ship live).
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md (new subsection: 'Non-Tailwind rendering surfaces') + a new lib/brand-html-constants.ts consumed by route.ts and lib/email-templates/*
findings.enforcement: gate: extend the existing A1 hardcoded-hex check to explicitly include app/api/**/*.ts in its strict (blocking) scope, since it is currently only caught in report mode

findings.title: Transactional emails render in colors from a retired, pre-B&W-pivot brand era with no link to LOCKFILE
findings.principle: Every hex literal inside lib/email-templates/*.ts and lib/email.ts must be one of the LOCKFILE §1 hex values, pulled from a single exported EMAIL_COLORS constant, never typed by hand inside a template string. A rebrand or token retirement must fail CI if an email template still contains an old hex.
findings.why: Email is often the customer's first and most memorable touchpoint (booking confirmations, salon-claim invites, loyalty rewards), and unlike a web page it cannot be fixed with a hot patch after the fact once sent; a customer who gets a teal-and-coral email while the live site is black-white-and-blue reads as two different, less trustworthy companies.
findings.local_evidence: lib/email-templates/off-peak.ts line 20-26 uses `#1A1A2E` (body text, not s-ink #0A0A0A), `#FF6B6B` (h2, not s-error #DC2626 or s-love), and `#38B2AC` (CTA button background, a teal that was explicitly retired in the V2-to-V3 B&W pivot and does not exist as any current token). lib/email.ts line 372 uses `#4ECDC4` (another cyan/teal) for a 'Salon jetzt beanspruchen' CTA button, line 576/584-587/714-717 use `#FAF6EF` (a warm cream not in the current cool-neutral s-bg table) for message/reward highlight boxes even while the SAME email correctly uses `#0A0A0A` for text (line 714), and line 632-635 uses `#FEF3C7`/`#D4870A` for an allergy-alert box that match neither s-warning.bg `#FDF6E7` nor s-warning.text `#B45309`.
findings.absence_proof: grep -ni 'email' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md _design-system/TASTE_LOG.md _design-system/REMOVED.md -> zero governance hits (the one SOURCE.md hit is about a form's email-input styling, not transactional email). grep -l 's-ink\|s-accent\|tailwind\|LOCKFILE' lib/email-templates/*.ts -> zero files reference the design system in any way.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md (new subsection under §1: 'Email surfaces') + lib/email-colors.ts as the single source
findings.enforcement: gate: a lightweight scan over lib/email-templates/*.ts and lib/email.ts for hex literals not present in the LOCKFILE-derived allowlist, run in the same drift-check pass

findings.title: The same #6B6B6B grey is reachable through four different token names with no naming-grammar rule to prevent it
findings.principle: A design token's variant (secondary/tertiary/hover/deep) is expressed exactly ONE way per token family: either as a nested Tailwind object key (`s-ink.secondary`) or as a flat hyphen-suffixed sibling token (`s-ink-2`), never both for the same value. When a variant is renamed or collapsed onto another value, the old spelling is deleted from tailwind.config.js in the same change, not left as a second live name for the identical hex.
findings.why: A token system's entire job is to make 'what color is this and why' answerable by one grep. When one value has multiple legitimate spellings, a future recolor of that grey requires finding and editing every spelling correctly, code review cannot tell whether two different class names are intentionally different shades or accidentally the same, and drift-checking rules (which match by name) silently under- or over-count real usage.
findings.local_evidence: tailwind.config.js line 131 defines `s-ink: { DEFAULT: "#0A0A0A", secondary: "#6B6B6B", tertiary: "#6B6B6B", disabled: "#C5C8C4" }`, and lines 132-133 separately define `s-ink-2: "#6B6B6B"` and `s-ink-3: "#6B6B6B"` -- the exact same hex, four names (`text-s-ink-secondary`, `text-s-ink-tertiary`, `text-s-ink-2`, `text-s-ink-3`). Live usage counts: s-ink-2 appears in 384 files, s-ink-3 in 196 files, s-ink-secondary in 1 file, s-ink-tertiary in 0 files -- so two of the four spellings (s-ink-2 and s-ink-3) are both actively growing in parallel today with zero semantic difference between them, per the tailwind.config.js comment itself ('V3-D138: collapsed onto ink-2').
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'naming\|grammar' _design-system/SOURCE.md -> only hits are 'card grammar' (§8) and 'state grammar' (§10), both about component structure, not token names. No section anywhere defines whether a token variant should be a nested key or a flat suffix.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md §1 (add a 'Token naming grammar' rule) and a one-time cleanup PR collapsing s-ink-tertiary/s-ink.tertiary into s-ink-2 sitewide
findings.enforcement: gate: extend RETIRED_TOKENS-style detection to flag any NEW usage of s-ink-3 or s-ink.tertiary/s-ink-secondary as drift once the LOCKFILE rule is written

findings.title: No automated contrast-ratio check exists anywhere; every WCAG contrast claim in the docs is a one-time manual assertion
findings.principle: Any NEW text/background color pairing introduced anywhere in the codebase (a token combo, a status chip, an email highlight box) must pass through a computed WCAG contrast check before shipping: the actual rendered foreground and background hex, contrast ratio computed programmatically, checked against 4.5:1 for text under 24px/19px-bold and 3:1 for larger text and non-text UI (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 and 1.4.11), measured on the RENDERED page, never assumed from the token pair's documented value at the time it was picked.
findings.why: LOCKFILE.md and SOURCE.md contain real contrast math (e.g. SOURCE.md:169 computing s-accent-on-white at ~3.7:1 and flagging it fails AA for normal body text), which proves the team already knows contrast can fail silently -- but that math was done once by hand for a handful of pairings. Every new component that pairs an existing token in a NEW combination (a pale bg the token was never tested against, a smaller font size than the original pairing assumed) inherits zero of that verification.
findings.local_evidence: SOURCE.md line 169 computes text-s-accent #276EF1 on white at ~3.7:1 by hand and flags it FAILS AA for normal body text; RATIONALE.md section 4 similarly hand-computes text-white on s-brand #16A34A at ~3.6:1. Both are one-time manual calculations frozen in prose comments at the moment the token pair was picked, with no script that could re-run them when a new component pairs those same tokens against a different background or at a different size.
findings.absence_proof: find . -iname '*contrast*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' returns only public/solen-weight-contrast-variants.html (a font-weight mockup, not a color-contrast tool). grep -n 'contrast' .claude/skills/solen-drift-check/scripts/check.py returns zero hits -- the drift-checker that DOES compute other things mechanically (hex allowlists, retired tokens, raw palette colors) has no contrast math at all. CLAUDE.md's own binary-triggers table fires a measurement tool for pixel/layout complaints but nothing for a color-contrast complaint.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: RATIONALE.md section 4 documents the WCAG contrast FORMULA and cites specific ratios for specific token pairs at the time they were locked (e.g. text-white on s-brand #16A34A = ~3.6:1, the s-accent-on-white 3.7:1 case). That is a point-in-time manual calculation, not a reusable, re-runnable check.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new scripts/check-contrast.mjs (or a rule inside solen-drift-check) + reference from _design-system/SOURCE.md's contrast paragraphs
findings.enforcement: gate: computed-contrast-gate -- given a `text-<token> bg-<token>` (or inline style) pairing and the resolved font-size/weight, compute the real ratio and block if it is under the applicable WCAG floor

findings.title: About a third of the defined color tokens have zero live usage, and nothing ever prunes them
findings.principle: Any color token with zero matches across app/, components/, components-legacy/, and lib/ for two consecutive quarterly design-system audits gets deleted from tailwind.config.js, not just moved to a RETIRED comment. A token definition that nothing renders is not neutral: it is a landmine for the next agent who greps tailwind.config.js, sees a plausible-sounding name, and assumes it is safe to use.
findings.why: tailwind.config.js's colors block has grown additively for months (the file's own comments document V2-D48 through V3-D470 eras) with almost no subtraction. A config that only grows eventually makes 'what colors exist' unanswerable without reading 250 lines of comments, which is the exact problem LOCKFILE.md was created to solve for the rest of the design system (LOCKFILE.md's own opening paragraph: 'without literal locked values... every section is locally accurate but the whole site feels stitched together').
findings.local_evidence: Of the 47 distinct top-level s- tokens defined in tailwind.config.js, a systematic per-token grep across app/components/components-legacy/lib found ZERO usage (not even in a comment) for 17 of them: s-amber-text, s-atm-bone, s-atm-butter, s-atm-cream, s-atm-sage, s-atm-terra, s-butter, s-cat-barbershop, s-cat-barbershop-text, s-cat-coiffeur, s-cat-coiffeur-text, s-cat-nails, s-cat-nails-text, s-cat-spa, s-cat-spa-text, s-chart-1, s-cream. That is 36 percent of the defined token surface rendering nothing anywhere, most of it (the atm-* and cat-* families) already explicitly named RETIRED in LOCKFILE.md months ago yet still physically present in the config with full multi-line historical comments.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'prune\|deprecat\|delete.*token\|token.*audit\|quarterly' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md _design-system/SOURCE.md _design-system/CANON.md -> no hits for any scheduled cleanup process. The RETIRED section documents WHAT is dead but never triggers actual deletion from tailwind.config.js.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the RETIRED section of LOCKFILE.md correctly identifies most of these families as dead in prose, and DRIFT_LEDGER.md exists for a different kind of drift (re-invented structure). Neither one deletes the token definition itself or schedules its removal.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md (add: 'RETIRED tokens are deleted from tailwind.config.js, not commented, after one quarter with zero usages') + tailwind.config.js cleanup PR
findings.enforcement: checklist: add a token-pruning line item to whatever periodic design-system audit already exists (consistency system / drift-check cadence)

findings.title: A duplicated, off-palette hardcoded hex gradient array is copy-pasted across 4 dashboard files, invisible to enforcement because the whole route is scope-excluded
findings.principle: Any literal design value (a color, a gradient pair, a spacing constant) that appears identically in more than one file must be promoted to a single shared exported constant in the same change that introduces the second copy. Separately: a route excluded from the drift-check scan scope (via _rebuilt_routes.json) is not exempt from the §0.6 no-hardcoded-hex rule -- scope exclusion silences the REPORT, it does not authorize new violations, and pre-existing violations inside excluded routes still need a tracked backlog with an owner and a date, not permanent invisibility.
findings.why: A rule that can be silently opted out of by living in the right subdirectory is not a rule, it is a coin flip based on which routes happen to have been rebuilt. And four independent hand-typed copies of the same 5-color array guarantee the next rebrand misses at least one of them, because nothing signals they are supposed to be identical.
findings.local_evidence: The identical literal `["from-[#276EF1] to-[#1B4DCB]", "from-[#F0A868] to-[#C0524A]", "from-[#16A34A] to-[#0E7A37]", "from-[#8B5CF6] to-[#6D28D9]", "from-[#EC4899] to-[#BE185D]"]` (an avatar-initial gradient palette) is hand-typed in app/[locale]/dashboard/page.tsx:85-86, app/[locale]/dashboard/clients/page.tsx:55-59, app/[locale]/dashboard/bookings/page.tsx:51-52, and app/[locale]/dashboard/staff/page.tsx:18-19. Six of the ten distinct hex values used (#1B4DCB, #F0A868, #C0524A, #8B5CF6, #6D28D9, #EC4899, #BE185D) are not in check.py's ALLOWED_HEX list and match no token in LOCKFILE §1-3 (purple/pink/terracotta hues outside the documented semantic palette). check.py's A1 hardcoded-hex rule would flag every one of these as a hard finding, but `_design-system/_rebuilt_routes.json` has zero dashboard entries, and CLAUDE.md documents that the drift-check 'respects `_rebuilt_routes.json` so legacy un-rebuilt routes don't drown signal' -- meaning these four files sit in a scanning blind spot by design.
findings.absence_proof: grep -i dashboard _design-system/_rebuilt_routes.json -> zero hits, confirming the exclusion. grep -rn 'scope.exclu\|un-rebuilt.*floor\|legacy.*hex.*allow' _design-system/LOCKFILE.md CLAUDE.md -> no rule states what IS and ISN'T allowed to accumulate inside an excluded route.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: §0.6 of LOCKFILE.md bans hardcoded hex system-wide in principle, and check.py's A1 rule is mechanically capable of catching this exact case. The gap is the un-rebuilt-route scope exclusion having no counterpart floor and no DRY/de-duplication rule for repeated literals.
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md §0.6 (add the scope-exclusion caveat) + a new lib/avatar-gradients.ts shared constant + _design-system/_rebuilt_routes.json entry once fixed
findings.enforcement: gate: run check.py's A1/A15 rules unconditionally (ignoring _rebuilt_routes.json) at least in report mode for hex specifically, since color drift is higher-risk than duration/easing drift

findings.title: The multi-series chart-color formula (OKLCH hue-stepping) is documented in prose with zero reference implementation
findings.principle: Any color-derivation FORMULA written into LOCKFILE (not a fixed hex, but a rule like 'derive hues in OKLCH from s-accent, hue stepped +25-30 per series') must ship as a small exported utility function in the same change, with its output values recorded as a worked example in the doc. A formula with no code either gets reimplemented differently by every future builder, or gets skipped because nobody wants to hand-compute OKLCH.
findings.why: The whole reason a numeric rule beats 'pick nice-looking colors' is that it's supposed to be reproducible. A rule that requires manual OKLCH math with no helper function will, in practice, either not be followed (the next dashboard chart just picks Tailwind palette colors, which is exactly what A15 exists to forbid) or be followed inconsistently, defeating the 'perceptually even, no neon-green-next-to-dull-blue' goal the rule states as its purpose.
findings.local_evidence: LOCKFILE.md line 103 (the Chart-grey section) states: 'when a dashboard chart needs >2 DISTINCT series (not hierarchy), derive hues in OKLCH from `s-accent` -- fixed lightness+chroma, hue stepped +25-30 per series.' `grep -rln oklch lib app components` (case-insensitive) returns zero files anywhere in the codebase -- no function, no constant, no CSS custom property implements this.
findings.absence_proof: find lib -iname '*color*' -o -iname '*oklch*' -> zero results. grep -rln 'oklch' lib app components -> zero results.
findings.existing_coverage: none beyond the prose rule itself
findings.where_it_should_live: lib/chart-colors.ts (new) + LOCKFILE.md's chart-grey section, replacing the prose formula with a call to the function and its worked-example output
findings.enforcement: checklist item on the next dashboard chart build: 'multi-series color comes from lib/chart-colors.ts, never hand-picked'

findings.title: No ceiling, or even a tracked count, on the total number of color tokens
findings.principle: The design system tracks and states its current color-token count (e.g. in LOCKFILE.md's header) and treats any PR that pushes the LIVE (non-retired) token count up without an owner-named reason as a flag for design review, the same way the radius/duration/easing systems already cap their own vocabularies to a small fixed set (LOCKFILE §4/§12 style closed lists).
findings.why: Every other governed axis in this system (radius, duration, easing, the neutral 'closed-inventory' hairline/surface table) is explicitly capped to a small enumerated set with a stated reason ('so nobody eyeballs a new radius per component'). Color is the one axis where the count is allowed to run open-ended, and it already has: 47 top-level tokens (many with 3-5 sub-keys, so 100+ addressable class names) is a large surface for a system whose stated goal is an '80/17 neutral+ink' palette with one sparse blue accent.
findings.local_evidence: `grep -oE '\"s-[a-zA-Z0-9-]+\"' tailwind.config.js | sort -u | wc -l` = 47 distinct top-level tokens today (verified count), against a design mandate (CLAUDE.md taste rule 3, LOCKFILE §1) of '~80% neutral, ~17% ink, blue sparse' -- a two-or-three-hue-family system. RATIONALE.md line 362 explicitly names 'keeping the token count small' as a design FORCE for the radius system but the equivalent sentence does not exist anywhere for color.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'token count\|how many token\|number of colou\|palette size\|too many token' _design-system/*.md _design-system/research/*.md -> only one hit, and it is about the RADIUS token count (RATIONALE.md:362), not color.
findings.existing_coverage: none for color specifically; the pattern exists for radius/duration/easing
findings.where_it_should_live: _design-system/LOCKFILE.md §1 (add current count + a stated ceiling or growth-review trigger)
findings.enforcement: checklist: any PR to tailwind.config.js's colors block that adds a token must state in the commit message which existing token it replaces or why net growth is justified

findings.title: No forced-colors / prefers-contrast handling anywhere outside one narrow glass-control note
findings.principle: Core CSS (app/globals.css) declares a `@media (forced-colors: active)` block that lets Windows/Edge High Contrast Mode substitute system colors on backgrounds, borders, and icons that currently rely on Solen's own hex tokens, so that color-dependent affordances (selected-state grey fills, status chips, hairlines) do not visually disappear for a user who has turned on OS-level forced colors.
findings.why: Forced-colors mode is a real, standards-track accessibility feature (part of the same WCAG-adjacent 'don't rely on author-specified color' family the system already partially honors via CVD redundancy) that specifically affects users relying on Windows assistive tech; a system whose selected-state and status signaling already leans on subtle grey-fill differences (per the CLAUDE.md 'selected = calm GRAY fill' law) is exactly the kind of UI where forced-colors mode can silently erase state distinctions that are normally rescued by icon/weight redundancy for CVD users but not by browser-level color overrides.
findings.local_evidence: grep -n 'forced-colors\|prefers-contrast' app/globals.css -> zero results. The only mention anywhere in the design system is _design-system/CONTROL_ELEVATION.md line 81, scoped narrowly to `prefers-contrast: more` for FROST_GLASS surfaces becoming 'a near-solid background + a defined border-s-border edge' -- nothing addresses the broader forced-colors media feature or non-glass surfaces.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rni 'forced-colors\|forced colors\|high contrast\|prefers-contrast' _design-system CLAUDE.md app/globals.css _rules -> only the one CONTROL_ELEVATION.md glass-specific hit.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: CONTROL_ELEVATION.md covers prefers-contrast for glass controls specifically. Forced-colors mode (a distinct, Windows-specific media feature) and the rest of the UI (buttons, chips, hairlines, selected states) are uncovered.
findings.enforcement: checklist item on the next accessibility pass; low-frequency enough not to need a hard gate
